analysis.one_liner: Lets Congress kill batches of an outgoing president's regulations with a single vote.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 238-184 on January 4, 2017, with all voting Republicans in favor, but the Senate never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, Congress can strike down a federal regulation only one at a time, through a separate resolution for each rule. This bill would let Congress bundle every regulation an agency issued in the final year of a president's term into one joint resolution and wipe them all out together, with the fast-track procedures of the Congressional Review Act — no debate, no amendments. It passed the House one day after it was introduced and died without a Senate vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries facing federal regulation — on pollution, workplace safety, financial practices, and consumer protection — would gain a fast, low-friction way to have many costly rules erased at once. The majority party in Congress also gains a standing tool: whenever a president of the other party leaves office, one vote can dispose of that administration's final-year rules without any per-rule scrutiny.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Congressional Review Act so a single joint resolution can disapprove multiple 'midnight' rules — regulations submitted in the last 60 legislative days of a president's final term — instead of requiring one resolution per rule.

Under the Congressional Review Act, each disapproval resolution gets expedited floor consideration with limited debate and no amendments, so bundling many rules together still guarantees each one a vote while removing any individual scrutiny.

analysis.who_pays: Whoever relied on the bundled rules: people exposed to pollution, unsafe workplaces, or financial and consumer abuses lose those protections when a package of rules is voided, and they get no separate hearing on each one.

drawbacks.text: Bundling removes per-rule scrutiny: a member who supports 90 rules in a package and opposes 10 must vote for or against the whole batch at once.

House Democrats warned the bill could sweep in healthcare protections: their motion to exempt rules that bar insurance discrimination based on gender or preexisting conditions, or that make healthcare more affordable, failed 183-236.
Supporters' good-faith argument is that lame-duck administrations issue rules with reduced accountability, and the one-at-a-time Congressional Review Act procedure is too slow to police them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated aim — checking end-of-term rulemaking — is legitimate, but the mechanism is a blunt mass-repeal tool. The value depends entirely on which rules a majority chooses to bundle; nothing in the bill weighs a rule's benefits against its costs or subjects any single rule to debate. The Senate never weighed it at all.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it the day after introduction, but the Senate sent it to its Homeland Security committee, which never acted on it, and the Congress ended without a Senate vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress, one month before the end of the Obama administration's term.
It passed the House the next day, January 4, 2017, 238-184, with 234 of 240 voting Republicans in favor and 4 of 193 voting Democrats.

A motion by Rep. Kathy Castor to require an amendment exempting rules that bar insurance discrimination based on gender or preexisting condition, or that make healthcare more affordable, failed 183-236, with no Republicans in support.

The Senate received the bill on January 5, 2017, and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee; the record shows no further Senate action through the end of the 115th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people kept the final-term rules intact, since nothing became law; regulated industries remain subject to the Obama-era rules the bill was built to erase in bulk. Congress did later repeal individual rules using the existing one-at-a-time procedure, but no package repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept its regulatory protections

for.name: Darrell Issa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the Congress; it reached the House floor the next day under a rule providing one hour of debate.

against.name: Kathy Castor
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to exempt rules banning insurance discrimination based on gender or preexisting conditions and rules making healthcare more affordable.

against.name: 184 of 193 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage and 183 voted for the motion to recommit.

against.name: Ron Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill on January 5, 2017, and never reported it or scheduled action; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: On passage, 234 of 240 voting Republicans voted yes while only 4 of 193 Democrats did; on the motion to recommit, 0 of 235 voting Republicans joined 183 Democrats.

industries.note: A bundled disapproval can void many pollution, workplace-safety, and financial rules with one vote and no per-rule debate, cutting their compliance costs at the public's expense.
The bill creates a permanent fast-track tool for whichever party holds Congress to erase the prior administration's final-year rules in bulk, consolidating procedural power over regulation.
Agencies' end-of-term rules become far easier to erase, weakening their output; the public relies on many of those same rules, so the agencies' interest here runs with ordinary people's.
